articles.title: How Much Should a Digital Product Cost? I Asked AI, Studied the Market, and Changed How I Think About Pricing
articles.excerpt: When I recently finished building a paid version of my small product, CutDone (where users create and customize printable goal lists), I ran into a question that looked simple at first: How much shoul…
articles.body: When I recently finished building a paid version of my small product, CutDone (where users create and customize printable goal lists), I ran into a question that looked simple at first: How much should I charge? Should it be $2.99? $3.99? $4.99? $5.99? I originally thought pricing was mostly a matter of intuition. Pick a number that feels reasonable and move on. But after discussing it with AI and looking at similar products across the web, I realized that pricing is much deeper than I had thought. And surprisingly mathematical. CutDone Is Not a Zero-Cost Product It would be wrong to say a digital product costs nothing. There are real fixed costs: time spent developing it, domain costs, infrastructure, maintenance, testing, and future customer support.

Each week I write up what I shipped, what broke, and what fixing it taught me. articles.body: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample A date bomb is a test that passes today and fails on a later date: an expiry check, a weekly cycle, a cutoff someone wrote as a fixed day. My project has a small tool for finding them. It moves today forward by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 30 and 100 days and runs the whole test suite at each date. Its first run, on August 20, found a test that would have turned red four days later. October 8 I opened the tool while looking for material for a post.

articles.title: I Tested 5 Proxy Types for Web Scraping — Here's What Actually Matters
articles.excerpt: Last month I rebuilt a scraping pipeline that had been limping along on a bargain-bin datacenter proxy plan. The symptoms were familiar to anyone who's done this at any scale: success rate hovering ar…
articles.body: Last month I rebuilt a scraping pipeline that had been limping along on a bargain-bin datacenter proxy plan. The symptoms were familiar to anyone who's done this at any scale: success rate hovering around 60%, CAPTCHAs on every third session, and a monthly bill that made no sense relative to the data we were actually collecting. So I did what any reasonable developer would do: I spent two weeks testing every proxy type I could get my hands on against the same set of targets, with the same code, and wrote down what actually happened. This post is the write-up. No affiliate nonsense, no "top 10 providers" list — just what each proxy type is, when it works, when it fails, and the code patterns that matter regardless of which type you pick.

articles.title: Forkpath: Change One Moment in History, Then Let the AI Do the Homework
articles.excerpt: What I Built Forkpath is an alternate-history explorer. You type one sentence ("What if the Ming treasure fleets kept sailing?"), pick when it happens, and an AI writer maps out what follows, event by…
articles.body: What I Built Forkpath is an alternate-history explorer. You type one sentence ("What if the Ming treasure fleets kept sailing?"), pick when it happens, and an AI writer maps out what follows, event by event, as a branching tree with the odds at every fork. Writing good alternate history is a lot of work. You research the period, think through who wants what, follow second- and third-order effects, and keep half a dozen storylines consistent. Forkpath does that homework for you. You type one line, lean back, and watch the timeline grow. What it gives you: 🌳 A map, not a story. Every event is a node. Where outcomes are genuinely uncertain, the writer branches and gives each branch a likelihood. A Most likely view fades every path history probably did not take. 🧵 Parallel streams.

articles.body: This year's open-world RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker and its myriad choices got me thinking: What does it really mean for your choices to matter in a video game? Typically, we think it's a good use of branching narratives when you have a properly big, dramatic effect on how things play out or when you have hundreds of endings. Just look at how so much attention on Baldur's Gate 3 focused on its endings or, years before, how everyone tended to ignore the smaller ways the Mass Effect trilogy changed across three games in favor of looking at the restrictive outcomes in Mass Effect 3 .

articles.title: 8 Classic PlayStation Adventure Games that are Barely Playable Today
articles.excerpt: From Tomb Raider to Silent Hill, eight classic PlayStation games whose tank controls, cameras, or lost code make them hard to play today
articles.body: If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

articles.body: Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell. One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi , when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services . You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set.

articles.title: Japan launches historic MMX sample-return mission to Mars' moon Phobos (video)
articles.excerpt: Japan just launched an epic mission to Mars' moons that could make history as the first spacecraft to return to Earth from the Red Planet — and it plans to come back with samples onboard.
articles.body: Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20). The JAXA ( Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency )-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 19, 2016: Europe's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli lander arrive at Mars
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli arrived at Mars! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars ! ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars , and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

The software performs finite element modeling to support shock and vibration analysis and ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces before launch, strengthening mission safety in the process. articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
